paperInfo.subject: Agriculture
sourceBasis: ZIMSEC-style assessment formats and recurring syllabus areas
Original questions generated for this bank; not transcriptions of past papers
paperInfo.note: Original practice questions aligned to Agriculture syllabus coverage. They do not reproduce copyrighted past-paper text.

questions.questionText: An enterprise has fixed costs of $18,000, variable costs of $42,000 and output revenue of $75,000. Calculate gross margin and net farm income for this enterprise, assuming no other costs.
questions.correctAnswer: Gross margin = $33,000; net farm income = $15,000.

questions.questionText: Explain cation exchange capacity (CEC), identify two factors that influence it, and discuss its importance in nutrient management.
questions.correctAnswer: CEC is the capacity of soil colloids to retain and exchange positively charged ions. It is influenced by clay content/type and organic matter. Higher CEC generally permits greater retention of nutrient cations and can reduce leaching losses, while management must still consider pH and nutrient balance.
questions.explanation: Clay minerals and humus carry negative charges that retain exchangeable cations such as Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺ and NH₄⁺.

questions.questionText: Describe the relationship between photosynthesis, respiration and net dry-matter accumulation in a crop. Explain how environmental stress can alter the balance.
questions.correctAnswer: Photosynthesis fixes carbon into organic compounds while respiration releases energy by oxidising substrates. Net biomass gain depends on carbon fixed minus respiratory losses. Drought, extreme temperature or nutrient stress can reduce photosynthesis and/or increase maintenance costs, lowering net accumulation.
questions.explanation: Crop growth is a balance between assimilate production and respiratory consumption.

questions.questionText: Outline a plant-breeding programme for improving drought tolerance in a maize population. Include selection, testing and release stages.
questions.correctAnswer: Define target trait and environment; select suitable diverse parents; cross or recombine; screen segregating populations under controlled drought stress; select superior lines/plants; replicate multi-location trials; evaluate yield stability and agronomic traits; maintain seed and release the improved variety after appropriate evaluation.
questions.explanation: Effective breeding combines a clearly defined target phenotype with repeated selection and multi-environment evaluation.

questions.questionText: Discuss integrated pest management (IPM) for a major field crop. Your answer should include monitoring, cultural, biological and chemical measures and explain why pesticide resistance should be managed.
questions.correctAnswer: Monitor pest populations and crop damage; use resistant varieties, rotation, sanitation and appropriate planting dates; conserve or introduce natural enemies; use selective pesticides only when justified by thresholds; rotate modes of action and use correct rates to slow resistance evolution.
questions.explanation: IPM combines compatible methods and reserves chemical control for economically justified situations.

questions.questionText: Explain the difference between genotype, phenotype and genotype × environment interaction, and discuss why G×E matters when selecting livestock.
questions.correctAnswer: Genotype is genetic constitution; phenotype is observed performance resulting from genotype and environment; G×E occurs when genotypes respond differently across environments. It matters because rankings of animals can change between production systems, so selection should use relevant environments and records.
questions.explanation: Selection decisions based on one environment may not predict performance elsewhere when G×E is substantial.

questions.questionText: A dairy ration supplies adequate crude protein but milk yield remains below target. Explain why crude-protein percentage alone may not guarantee adequate protein nutrition.
questions.correctAnswer: Protein supply depends on degradability, microbial protein synthesis, essential amino-acid supply, energy synchronisation, intake and digestibility. A ration can contain adequate crude protein yet lack metabolically available amino acids or energy needed for efficient microbial protein production.
questions.explanation: Ration formulation must consider nutrient supply and utilisation, not crude protein alone.

questions.questionText: Explain how the rumen enables cattle to use fibrous feeds. Include microbial fermentation, volatile fatty acids and microbial protein.
questions.correctAnswer: Rumen microbes ferment structural carbohydrates to volatile fatty acids, which supply much of the animal's energy. Microbes also synthesise protein from available nitrogen; microbial biomass later passes to the lower digestive tract where it is digested and supplies amino acids.
questions.explanation: Symbiotic microbial fermentation allows ruminants to exploit cellulose-rich feeds.

questions.questionText: Design a grazing plan for a farm experiencing pasture degradation. Include stocking rate, rest periods, forage monitoring and actions during drought.
questions.correctAnswer: Estimate carrying capacity and adjust stocking rate; divide grazing areas where feasible; use planned rotation with adequate recovery; monitor herbage mass and ground cover; protect vulnerable areas; provide conserved forage and destock or reduce grazing pressure during drought.
questions.explanation: Pasture sustainability requires matching animal demand with forage supply over time.

questions.questionText: A tractor engine is losing power and producing excessive smoke. Describe a systematic diagnostic procedure before major components are replaced.
questions.correctAnswer: Check operator observations and service history; inspect fuel quality and filters; check air intake/filter; inspect fuel injection and cooling systems; check lubrication; test compression if indicated; use manufacturer specifications and isolate one fault at a time.
questions.explanation: Systematic diagnosis avoids unnecessary replacement and identifies simple causes first.

questions.questionText: Explain price elasticity of demand and discuss two implications for a farmer selling a highly perishable crop.
questions.correctAnswer: Price elasticity measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price. For a perishable crop, weak short-term storage and time pressure may reduce the farmer's bargaining power; grading, market timing, alternative outlets and value addition can improve marketing options.
questions.explanation: Elasticity is a percentage-based responsiveness concept; perishability affects marketing strategy and bargaining conditions.

questions.questionText: A farm has two enterprises. Enterprise A has a gross margin of $18,000 using 30 hectares; Enterprise B has a gross margin of $14,000 using 14 hectares. Calculate gross margin per hectare for each and interpret the result.
questions.correctAnswer: A: $600/ha. B: $1,000/ha. B gives the higher gross margin per hectare, although final choice should also consider labour, capital, risk and other limiting resources.

questions.questionText: Discuss how soil organic matter influences soil structure, water relations, nutrient supply and biological activity.
questions.correctAnswer: Organic matter promotes aggregation and stable structure, improves water-holding capacity and infiltration, contributes nutrients through decomposition and supports diverse soil organisms. Its effects depend on quantity, quality and climate.
questions.explanation: Organic matter is central to many physical, chemical and biological soil functions.

questions.questionText: Explain how rainfall intensity, soil cover, slope and infiltration interact to determine erosion risk on a cultivated field.
questions.correctAnswer: High-intensity rainfall can exceed infiltration and generate runoff; bare soil is vulnerable to detachment; steeper slopes increase runoff velocity; good infiltration and surface cover reduce runoff and particle detachment. Therefore conservation measures target cover, infiltration and flow velocity.
questions.explanation: Erosion results from interacting rainfall energy, soil susceptibility and runoff processes.

questions.questionText: A researcher compares three fertiliser treatments using four replicated plots per treatment. Explain why replication, randomisation and a control are important, and state what a statistically significant treatment effect would mean.
questions.correctAnswer: Replication estimates experimental variability; randomisation reduces allocation bias; a control provides a baseline for comparison. A statistically significant effect indicates that the observed treatment differences are unlikely to be explained by random variation alone under the stated statistical model.
questions.explanation: Sound experimental design supports valid inference about treatment effects.

questions.questionText: Explain how rainfall intensity, soil cover, slope and infiltration interact to determine erosion risk on a cultivated field.

questions.questionText: An enterprise has fixed costs of $18,000, variable costs of $42,000 and output revenue of $75,000. Calculate gross margin and net farm income for this enterprise, assuming no other costs.

questions.questionText: Explain cation exchange capacity (CEC), identify two factors that influence it, and discuss its importance in nutrient management.

questions.questionText: Describe the relationship between photosynthesis, respiration and net dry-matter accumulation in a crop. Explain how environmental stress can alter the balance.

questions.explanation: Elasticity is a percentage-based responsiveness concept; perishability affects marketing strategy and bargaining conditions.

questions.questionText: A farm has two enterprises. Enterprise A has a gross margin of $18,000 using 30 hectares; Enterprise B has a gross margin of $14,000 using 14 hectares. Calculate gross margin per hectare for each and interpret the result.
questions.correctAnswer: A: $600/ha. B: $1,000/ha. B gives the higher gross margin per hectare, although final choice should also consider labour, capital, risk and other limiting resources.

questions.questionText: Discuss how soil organic matter influences soil structure, water relations, nutrient supply and biological activity.
questions.correctAnswer: Organic matter promotes aggregation and stable structure, improves water-holding capacity and infiltration, contributes nutrients through decomposition and supports diverse soil organisms. Its effects depend on quantity, quality and climate.
questions.explanation: Organic matter is central to many physical, chemical and biological soil functions.

questions.questionText: Explain how rainfall intensity, soil cover, slope and infiltration interact to determine erosion risk on a cultivated field.
questions.correctAnswer: High-intensity rainfall can exceed infiltration and generate runoff; bare soil is vulnerable to detachment; steeper slopes increase runoff velocity; good infiltration and surface cover reduce runoff and particle detachment. Therefore conservation measures target cover, infiltration and flow velocity.
questions.explanation: Erosion results from interacting rainfall energy, soil susceptibility and runoff processes.

questions.questionText: A researcher compares three fertiliser treatments using four replicated plots per treatment. Explain why replication, randomisation and a control are important, and state what a statistically significant treatment effect would mean.
questions.correctAnswer: Replication estimates experimental variability; randomisation reduces allocation bias; a control provides a baseline for comparison. A statistically significant effect indicates that the observed treatment differences are unlikely to be explained by random variation alone under the stated statistical model.
questions.explanation: Sound experimental design supports valid inference about treatment effects.
